questions.q: Why is a task-specific eval set still necessary even when standard benchmarks and LLM-as-judge comparisons are already being used?
options: It isn't necessary -- standard benchmarks always cover every product-specific need

A generic benchmark has no items testing a company's specific policies or product terminology, so a bespoke eval set is where 'does this model actually work for what we're shipping' gets answered directly
Task-specific eval sets are required by law for all AI products
LLM-as-judge comparisons automatically generate product-specific test items
questions.explain: Generic benchmarks and chat comparisons measure general capability, but they have no items built around a specific product's policies, terminology, or edge cases -- only a bespoke eval set can test that directly.

questions.q: What are the two recommended sources for examples in a task-specific eval set?
options: Only data purchased from a third-party vendor
Real, anonymized usage (queries or support tickets, filtered for sensitive data) supplemented with examples a domain expert writes to cover known edge cases
Randomly generated synthetic text with no connection to the actual product
Exclusively text copied from public benchmarks like MMLU
questions.explain: The lesson recommends sourcing from real anonymized product usage plus deliberately written domain-expert examples covering known failure modes, rather than relying on generic or synthetic sources.

questions.q: Why does each item in a task-specific eval set benefit from its own rubric and reference answer, rather than a generic 1-5 quality scale?
options: Generic scales are always more accurate than item-specific rubrics
A per-item rubric and reference answer make scoring criteria concrete and actionable for that specific scenario, usable by a human evaluator, an LLM judge, or an automated check
Reference answers are only useful for benchmarks like GSM8K, never for custom eval sets
Rubrics are unnecessary once a reference answer is provided
questions.explain: A per-item rubric and reference answer anchor scoring to the specifics of that scenario (such as citing the correct policy window), making evaluation concrete and consistent rather than relying on vague generic criteria.

questions.q: What is the Goodhart's law risk associated with a task-specific eval set, and what are two defenses against it?
options: There is no risk -- a task-specific eval set can be optimized against indefinitely with no downside

Heavy iteration against the same fixed items risks overfitting to their quirks rather than real capability; defenses include periodically refreshing the set and holding out a slice never used during iterative development
The only defense is to delete the eval set entirely after one use
Goodhart's law only applies to public benchmarks, never to custom eval sets
questions.explain: Goodhart's law warns that optimizing directly against a fixed measure can degrade its value as an honest signal; refreshing the eval set and holding out an untouched slice for final checks are the recommended defenses.

questions.q: How does lm-evaluation-harness support task-specific eval sets alongside standard benchmarks like MMLU?
options: It does not support custom eval sets at all -- only predefined benchmarks

It supports custom tasks defined via YAML configuration pointing at a dataset and specifying scoring, allowing a task-specific eval set to run through the same tooling and regression suite as standard benchmarks
Custom eval sets require a completely separate, incompatible tool
lm-evaluation-harness only works with benchmarks that have no rubric or reference answer
questions.explain: lm-evaluation-harness allows defining custom tasks via YAML configuration, so a task-specific eval set can be run through the same tooling and regression process used for standard benchmarks like MMLU or GSM8K.
